unesco.title: Al-Razfa, a traditional performing art
unesco.description: Al-Razfa is a traditional performing art practised throughout the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. It is performed by men of all ages and classes during social occasions, such as weddings and national festivals. Male performers form two facing lines with dancers filling the space between. Led by the main singer, the two rows create a dual chorus, singing chants in an antiphonal manner to the accompaniment of drums and other instruments. Many chants are verses of traditional Nabati poetry, carefully selected to match the occasion. The dancers perform choreographed movements to the music while holding wooden replica rifles in their hands and in some cases, young girls swing their hair in time to the music. Originally performed as a communal celebration of victory, Al-Razfa is now widely popular as a form of entertainment. Practitioners have adapted musical instruments and composed melodies to interest younger audiences while maintaining the older expressions and oral traditions of the art. Performers may include heads of State and elders or very young children. Today, Al-Razfa is transmitted directly within the family through participation and observation at social occasions. The roles of individual performers are learnt by practice, while girls receive instruction from their mothers and older sisters.

profile.name: Al-Razfa
profile.tagline: Antiphonal Nabati poetry and choreographed rifle movements from the UAE and Oman.
profile.insight: Once a communal celebration of victory, Al-Razfa now unites generations in the UAE and Oman through antiphonal Nabati chants and the rhythmic manipulation of wooden replica rifles.
profile.profile: Al-Razfa is a traditional performing art practiced across the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman, characterized by two facing lines of men chanting antiphonal Nabati poetry. Dancers perform choreographed movements in the space between these lines, often wielding wooden replica rifles, while young girls may participate by swinging their hair. Originally a victory celebration, the art is now a popular social entertainment transmitted through family participation at weddings and national festivals.
profile.profile_long:
Al-Razfa is a traditional performing art deeply embedded in the social fabric of the United Arab Emirates and the Sultanate of Oman. Historically, the practice emerged as a communal celebration of victory, often performed following tribal wars or the return of men from successful pearl diving expeditions. Today, it has transitioned into a widely popular form of social entertainment, serving as a vital link between generations. The performance is inclusive, featuring participants ranging from heads of State and elders to very young children, all of whom contribute to the maintenance of this oral tradition.

The structure of an Al-Razfa performance is defined by its spatial arrangement and antiphonal vocal delivery. Male performers form two facing lines, creating a dual chorus that is led by a main singer. The space between these two rows serves as the stage for dancers who execute choreographed movements. These dancers frequently hold wooden replica rifles, which they manipulate in rhythm with the music. In some instances, young girls participate by standing near the performers and swinging their hair in time to the music, a gesture that adds a rhythmic visual element to the performance. The vocal component consists of chants, many of which are verses of traditional Nabati poetry, carefully selected to suit the specific occasion, such as a wedding or a national festival.

Transmission of the art form occurs directly within the family unit. Knowledge, skills, and values are passed down through observation and active participation at social gatherings. While the roles of individual performers are learned through practice, young girls receive instruction from their mothers and older sisters. This method of transmission ensures that the art remains a living tradition, even as practitioners adapt musical instruments and compose new melodies to engage younger audiences. By maintaining these older expressions alongside modern adaptations, the community preserves the heritage of the art while ensuring its continued relevance in contemporary society. The performance is not merely a display of skill but a reflection of the region's national identity and a means of fostering mutual understanding and peace among the people of the UAE and Oman.
